text: One unknown \(K\) means one equation, and the equation comes from the one rule every PDF must obey: total area 1, Theorem 4.2(c) [p. 125]. For part (b), the book's direct route from a PDF to a CDF is Theorem 4.2(b), integrating from the far left [p. 126].

label: (a)
title: The value of K, and the shape of the PDF
Turn the area rule into an equation for K

text: \(K\) controls how much the parabola \(b^2 + Kb + 1\) sags in the middle of its interval, but its value is not free: a PDF describes probability, and the probability of the whole sample space is 1. Theorem 4.2 turns that requirement into calculus:

name: PDF properties
text: For a continuous random variable \(X\) with PDF \(f_X(x)\): (a) \(f_X(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x\); (b) \(F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(u)\,du\); (c) \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\,dx = 1\).
Here \(f_B\) is zero outside \(0 < b \le 2\), so all the area sits in one integral over that interval:

title: Evaluate the integral and solve for K

steps.why: Antidifferentiate term by term; the constant 1 integrates to \(b\).
At \(b = 2\) the three terms give \(8/3\), \(2K\) and \(2\); at \(b = 0\) all are 0.
Theorem 4.2(c) says this area must be exactly 1.

text: So \(K\) comes out negative: with it, \(f_B(b) = b^2 - \frac{11}{6}b + 1\) on \(0 < b \le 2\), a parabola that starts at height 1, dips, and climbs again.

title: Check the result is a legal PDF

text: Setting the area to 1 was necessary but not sufficient: Theorem 4.2(a) also requires \(f_B \ge 0\) everywhere [p. 125]. This quadratic opens upward, so its smallest value on \((0, 2]\) is at the vertex, where its derivative \(2b - \frac{11}{6}\) is zero.

steps.why: The vertex of \(b^2 - \frac{11}{6}b + 1\) sits halfway along the dip.
Even the lowest point of the curve is above zero, so \(f_B \ge 0\) on all of \((0, 2]\).
The endpoint heights, for the sketch.

title: A PDF height above 1 is legal
text: At \(b = 2\) the curve reaches \(\frac{4}{3}\), taller than 1. The book points out that a PDF value is not a probability and need not lie between 0 and 1; only areas under the curve are probabilities [p. 125].

The plots here are the required sketches. If you take the MATLAB option the problem offers, fplot(@(b) b.^2 - (11/6)*b + 1, [0 2]) reproduces the PDF curve; add the zero pieces outside \((0, 2]\) if you draw the whole function.

label: (a)
text: \(K = -\frac{11}{6}\), so \(f_B(b) = b^2 - \frac{11}{6}b + 1\) on \(0 < b \le 2\) and 0 otherwise. The sketch shows the dip to \(\frac{23}{144}\) at \(b = \frac{11}{12}\) and the climb to \(\frac{4}{3}\) at \(b = 2\).

title: Integrate the PDF from 0 up to b

text: \(F_B(b) = P[B \le b]\) is the probability accumulated to the left of \(b\), which for a continuous random variable is the area under the PDF up to \(b\). The book recommends exactly this route when a problem starts from the PDF: find the CDF by means of Theorem 4.2(b) [p. 126]. Since \(f_B\) contributes nothing below 0, the lower limit is 0:

steps.why: Theorem 4.2(b), with \(t\) as the dummy variable so the upper limit \(b\) stays free.
Antidifferentiate; integration halves the power, so the coefficient \(\frac{11}{6}\) becomes \(\frac{11}{12}\).
Everything vanishes at the lower limit \(t = 0\).

text: To the left of 0 no area has accumulated, and past \(b = 2\) the accumulation is complete, so the CDF sits flat at 0 and at 1 on either side of the cubic:

The problem writes the support as \(0 < b \le 2\), open at 0 and closed at 2. For a continuous random variable this precision never matters: individual numbers have probability zero, so including or excluding an endpoint cannot change any probability [p. 127].

title: Check the ends, then the slope
text: Every CDF runs from 0 up to 1 [p. 121], and here \(F_B(2) = \frac{2^3}{3} - \frac{11}{12}(2^2) + 2 = 1\) with \(F_B(0^+) = 0\). Differentiating also returns the PDF, \(\frac{dF_B}{db} = b^2 - \frac{11}{6}b + 1 = f_B(b)\), as Definition 4.3 requires [p. 124]; the CDF is continuous everywhere but has a corner at \(b = 0\), where the PDF jumps from 0 to 1.

label: (b)
text: \(F_B(b) = 0\) for \(b \le 0\); \(F_B(b) = \frac{b^3}{3} - \frac{11}{12}b^2 + b\) for \(0 < b \le 2\); \(F_B(b) = 1\) for \(b > 2\). The curve rises smoothly from 0 to 1, flattening over the dip in the PDF near \(b = \frac{11}{12}\).
